claims.text: Low-temperature hydride decomposition in an inert atmosphere followed by rapid high-pressure consolidation will suppress oxygen uptake.
Suppressing oxygen uptake through the proposed process will prevent precipitation of brittle alpha-HCP phases.
The proposed hydride-decomposition and extrusion route will produce a dense bulk alloy.
The proposed route will maximize high-temperature yield strength.
A decomposition temperature below 600°C is below the onset of rapid oxidation for the relevant hydride precursors.
Ultra-high vacuum below 10^-6 mbar or argon containing less than 1 ppm oxygen is required to control oxygen uptake.
Extrusion pressure above 500 MPa is required for rapid consolidation of the decomposed precursor.
The proposed processing history will retain a metastable BCC solid solution.
Suppressed oxygen diffusion and rapid consolidation kinetics prevent nucleation of the brittle alpha-HCP phase.
Low-temperature hydride decomposition releases hydrogen.
Low-temperature decomposition provides insufficient thermal energy for significant oxygen diffusion from the atmosphere or crucible walls.
High-pressure extrusion densifies the alloy.
A rapid thermal history analogous to HVAF or LENS processing suppresses the thermodynamic driving force for alpha-HCP precipitation.
The rapid thermal history limits grain growth.
A fine-grained metastable BCC structure resists dislocation motion and crack initiation.
The processed bulk alloy will have porosity below 0.5%.
The processed alloy will contain no alpha-HCP phase detectable by XRD.
The processed alloy will have a ductile-to-brittle transition temperature below room temperature.
The processed alloy will have a yield strength exceeding 1000 MPa at 800°C.
Alpha-HCP formation is thermodynamically favored above 800°C in the targeted Group-IV-containing refractory HEAs.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is restricted to Group-IV-containing alloys such as Ti-, Zr-, or Hf-containing refractory HEAs, but the proposed falsification alloy Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 contains no Group IV element. It therefore does not directly test the stated material scope.
The predicted outcome requires porosity below 0.5%, whereas the experiment only falsifies the hypothesis above 1%; results between 0.5% and 1% violate the prediction without triggering falsification.
The predicted outcome requires no alpha-HCP detectable by XRD, whereas the falsification rule permits up to 5 vol% alpha-HCP without falsification.
